references.text: God warns of the flood that will destroy all flesh—the event that the covenant with Noah later guarantees will never happen again.
After the flood, God promises in His heart never to curse the ground again or strike down all living things, which prepares for the formal covenant oath to Noah.
God introduces the covenant He establishes with Noah, his descendants, and every living creature—the covenant whose content is elaborated in verse 11.
God confirms that He will remember His covenant, so that the waters shall never again become a flood that destroys all flesh.
God establishes an eternal covenant with Abraham and his descendants, demonstrating God's faithfulness to His covenant promises throughout history.
Isaiah refers directly to Noah's flood and God's oath that the waters will never again cover the earth, as a picture of His unfailing grace.
Peter reminds us of God's judgment by water in Noah's days, but emphasizes that the present world is reserved for judgment by fire—confirming that the flood will not happen again.
Direct allusion where Isaiah uses God's oath about the flood (Gen 9:11) as a guarantee that His wrath will not last forever.
Stylistic and theological parallel: God's 'never again' promise regarding the flood is used as a model for the promise of protection from enemies.
